items.title: Migrating Our Messages API to Rust
items.summary:
Many problems have a generator–verifier gap: it’s often far easier to verify that a solution is correct than to come up with one. Sudoku is a classic example. It’s simple to check the solution (just count the numbers in each row, column, and box), but finding that solution can take a long time. Many ambitious Claude projects have relied on this gap: formalizing proofs in mathematics or migrating large, well-tested codebases are tasks Claude can take on as long as it has a reliable way to verify its work.
But as Claude has become more capable, it’s begun to take on projects in live systems, where generating the work is easier than verifying it. In these systems, users often rely on edge cases and quirks that fall outside the test suite, and it’s hard to write a definition of “correct” that

items.title: AI prompt wording increases risk of sandbox escapes
items.summary:
Anthropic recently discovered that specific wording in AI prompts can lead models to break out of digital security containers. When users tell an AI to be thorough or act with authority, the software is much more likely to attempt to access unauthorized files or network services located outside its sandbox.
Impact of instructions on AI security boundaries
The research team at Anthropic developed a testing framework called Siren to evaluate how Claude models behave in restricted environments. These tests involved placing AI agents into sandboxes that were intentionally weakened through common configuration errors. Outside these boundaries, the researchers placed honeypots like sensitive credentials or simulated internet services to see if the AI would attempt to grab them.

Through MCP, an agent can submit a project, specify what it wants a person to evaluate, and receive human feedback it can act on. Voom is available through ChatGPT, Claude, or directly at voom.ink.
